title: Europe's Last Coal Plants Turn Profitable as Gas Hits 2022 Levels and Seoul Shifts Back to Coal
subhead: Lignite margins in Germany jumped from zero to as much as $72 per MWh this month, and South Korea's energy minister says Seoul must cut LNG use this winter — two signs that the gas crisis is being resolved by burning dirtier fuel, not more gas. Brent slipped to about $108 after its highest settle since May. China's storage at 80% full is the one real buffer.

sections.heading: Coal Is Back in the Merit Order — Profitably
sections.body:
Europe's surviving coal fleet is making money again. The lignite-to-power spread in Germany has risen to as much as $72 (64 euros) per megawatt-hour this month, against roughly zero a year ago, according to Energy Aspects estimates cited by Bloomberg and reported by OilPrice.com. Analyst Sabrina Kernbichler said the spreads are expected to stay high through March. Germany and Poland hold most of Europe's remaining operational or back-up-ready coal capacity, and coal is now doing grid-stability work that gas-fired plants cannot afford to do at current fuel costs.

The IEA's Coal Mid-Year Update 2026, cited in the same reporting, expects European coal demand of 276 million tons in 2026, down from 292 million last year but higher than previously forecast — explicitly because higher gas prices have slowed the decline in Germany and Poland, where spare coal capacity remains available.

Why the market cleared this way: LNG is barely moving out of the Strait of Hormuz, and LNG flows from the Middle East remain about 80% below last year's volumes even as crude flows have partially recovered. ING's head of commodities strategy Warren Patterson put it plainly in a note: 'Unfortunately for the natural gas market, we have not seen a similar recovery in LNG flows from the Persian Gulf as we have with oil.' European gas prices are trading at levels last seen in the 2022-2023 crisis.
sections.whyItMatters: The price signal is now pushing Europe's power system toward its most emissions-intensive assets at exactly the moment it is trying to legislate them out. Any EU decarbonisation timeline that assumed coal was already economically dead needs revisiting.

sections.heading: South Korea: 'We Must Somehow Reduce LNG Demand'
sections.body:
Asia's third-largest LNG buyer is making the same call in public. Climate, Energy and Environment Minister Kim Sungwhan told Bloomberg that Seoul will lean harder on coal and nuclear this winter and cut gas burn. 'In the short term, we are in a situation where we must somehow reduce LNG demand,' Kim said, adding that Korea must reduce gas usage by expanding renewables while 'more actively utilizing nuclear and coal power.'

This is a reversal of direction, not a wobble. Coal-fired supply in South Korea jumped 40% in April, the largest increase since August 2019, per market data cited by Reuters. The government has simultaneously announced a plan to invest as much as 1 quadrillion Korean won ($747 billion) in renewables, EVs and industrial decarbonisation through 2035 — an energy-security hedge being financed while the dirty fallback is restarted.

The bill is the reason. Research by Ember and Global Energy Monitor cited by OilPrice.com puts South Korea's annual fossil fuel import cost at about $133 billion at early-June 2026 spot prices — nearly six times the country's annual debt repayments and almost three times its defence spending. Qatar's supply is the missing piece: with Hormuz constrained and Ras Laffan still impaired, spot cargoes that avoid the strait are priced out of reach for baseload generation.
sections.whyItMatters: Korea is proving that 'energy security trumps the transition' is not a European or American rhetorical line — it is the actual operating rule for a major industrial democracy with no domestic hydrocarbons. Japan, Taiwan and India face the same arithmetic.

sections.heading: Brent's Pullback From a Five-Month High Is a Breather, Not a Turn
sections.body:
Brent crude fell $1.80, or 1.64%, to $108.06 a barrel early Monday, after settling Friday at its highest level since 19 May, according to Indian market reporting. WTI slipped 53 cents to $100.88. OilPrice.com's live board showed Brent near $108.0 and WTI near $100.7 at the time of writing, with Murban at $113.4 and heating oil at $4.82 a gallon — the distillate premium remains the story, not the crude headline.

The physical market is still tight underneath the paper move. Vitol's head of Asian operations Kieran Gallagher, speaking at an industry event and quoted by Reuters, said Middle East high-sulfur fuel oil exports are running at least 800,000 tons a month below pre-war levels, against a pre-war monthly average of 3.7 million tons per Kpler data. The HSFO premium for marine fuel has reached almost $50 per ton, up from $5.10 in late February, per LSEG data cited by Reuters. Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries have removed a further estimated 1 million tons per month, Gallagher said.

The knock-on is operational, not just financial: shipowners are paying record voyage costs and tying up working capital while waiting for the right grade at the right port, per an OilPrice.com analysis by Cyril Widdershoven published Sunday. Fujairah's fuel oil imports recovered to 2.6 million tons in Q3 from 845,000 tons in Q2, but September imports were still roughly half of February's level.
sections.whyItMatters: One day of crude selling does not repair a product market where refinery feedstock, bunker grade availability and freight risk are all impaired at once. The distillate and fuel oil spreads, not the Brent print, tell you how tight the system still is.

sections.heading: Europe's Storage Is the Weakest Link Going Into Winter
sections.body:
European gas storage sites were 74% full as of last week, compared with more than 86% for the same period across the previous five years, per Bloomberg data cited by OilPrice.com. In September the EU sat at roughly 67%, against a seasonal average near 80%, and Germany — holder of the bloc's largest capacity — is roughly half full and expected to miss its official 80% target this year, according to the Guardian and EU Institute for Security Studies figures reported by OilPrice.com.

The EU's 90%-by-1-November rule, introduced after the 2022 crisis, is now being flexed rather than met. Gas Infrastructure Europe data cited by Anadolu Agency showed EU storage at about 69% in mid-September; the European Commission has supported letting member states use a lower 80% target and meet it any time between 1 October and 1 December. Storage normally covers 25-30% of EU winter consumption, so a smaller buffer translates directly into higher price volatility on any cold snap. Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen has warned of a challenging winter with 'very high' oil and gas prices while saying no supply shortage is expected, and has proposed postponing methane-emission rules on energy imports to ease market pressure.

The accumulated cost is large: the EU is estimated to have paid an additional €100 billion for oil and gas so far this year, with extra energy costs since 2022 surpassing €900 billion, per EUISS analysis cited by OilPrice.com.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe enters winter with the thinnest buffer since 2022 and a storage mandate it has effectively relaxed. That leaves price, not policy, as the allocation mechanism for the next five months — and it makes the Russian-gas-for-peace idea Washington floated last week harder for Brussels to dismiss on principle alone.

sections.heading: China's 80% Storage Is the Only Large Buffer in the System
sections.body:
China's underground gas storage was 80% full at the end of September, according to Rystad Energy analyst Xiong Wei, cited by Bloomberg via OilPrice.com. Chinese LNG buyers moved early to build inventories after the Iran war began, and the pay-off is that the world's largest LNG importer may buy less spot supply this winter — relief for every other Asian and European buyer competing for cargoes that avoid Hormuz.

A second variable is working in the same direction: weather models point to a super El Niño raising winter temperatures across South Korea, Japan and parts of China, cutting heating demand and leaving more cargoes for Europe through January 2027.

Beijing is also profiting from the disruption rather than merely absorbing it. PetroChina International, the trading arm of Asia's largest oil and gas producer, is set to book more than $3 billion (20 billion yuan) in gross trading profit for 2026, according to trade sources cited by Reuters — a record, driven by volatility and arbitrage across crude, fuels and LNG. PetroChina posted record first-half profit attributable to shareholders of $15.5 billion, up 22% year over year. European majors are in the same trade: Shell's indicative Q3 refining margin rose to $42 per barrel from $24 in Q2, and TotalEnergies has flagged a windfall from refining margins and LNG prices.
sections.whyItMatters: China's storage position and a warm El Niño forecast are the two things standing between Europe and a repeat of 2022 — neither is under European control. The windfall accruing to PetroChina and the refiners also shows who is being paid for the volatility.

sections.heading: The Nord Stream Case Reaches a German Courtroom
sections.body:
A German court began trying former Ukrainian officer Serhii Kuznetsov on 14 October over the September 2022 sabotage of the Nord Stream pipelines, per RFE/RL reporting via OilPrice.com. Prosecutors have identified seven Ukrainian suspects but only one in the dock, charged as an accomplice to a war crime. The indictment, summarised by the German Federal Prosecutor's Office, alleges that in late February 2022 he and other military personnel 'on behalf of state authorities in Ukraine' developed the plan, with the aim of permanently halting gas deliveries and preventing Russia from financing its war with gas revenue.

Kyiv denies involvement, and prosecutors have not publicly established a role for Ukraine's political leadership. German outlets ARD, Sueddeutsche Zeitung and Die Zeit, reporting on the indictment, said investigators recorded a call from custody in Italy in which Kuznetsov said a lawyer advised him to admit this had been 'an official military operation' and that his commander should state they were not 'two crazy military men.' His Italian lawyer, Nicola Canestrini, has dismissed the significance, saying there is no smoking gun.

The pipeline itself has become a live commercial question again only in the last week, after US envoys proposed resuming Russian gas flows to Europe as part of a peace settlement. The trial gives that debate a legal frame: if the destruction of German energy infrastructure is being litigated as an act carried out on behalf of a state that Germany arms, the politics of any restart get considerably harder for Berlin and easier for Moscow.
sections.whyItMatters: A sworn public accounting of who blew up Europe's flagship gas link arrives the same month Washington is floating Russian gas as a peace-deal currency. Testimony will shape German domestic support for Kyiv and Moscow's argument that the gas relationship was destroyed by others, not by Russian pressure.

sections.heading: Rationing Is Already Arriving in South Asia
sections.body:
Pakistan is the clearest case of the LNG crunch turning into a consumer crisis. Masood Nabi, chief executive of state importer Pakistan LNG Limited, told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh that winter will be challenging because the bottleneck is not gas availability but severely disrupted transit through the Strait of Hormuz, per Upstream reporting cited by OilPrice.com.

The numbers are stark. Pakistan sourced 99% of its LNG imports from Qatar under term contracts last year; Qatar declared force majeure in March after Iranian strikes damaged the Ras Laffan export hub. Some Qatari cargoes have reached Pakistan following direct Iranian assurances on transit safety, but Islamabad now needs about 10 additional spot cargoes for November 2026 to February 2027 at roughly double the Qatari contract price, and will pay in excess of $1 billion to secure winter supply. Spot purchases have already pushed power generation costs up sharply.

There is a security dimension beyond price: a state with a single dominant supplier, a single transit chokepoint and no strategic storage is structurally dependent on the goodwill of the belligerent controlling the strait. Iran has demonstrated it can open and close that tap country by country.
sections.whyItMatters: Pakistan's winter is a preview of how the Hormuz crisis is being paid for outside the wealthy importing blocs — in blackouts, in doubled spot prices, and in bilateral dependence on Iran's discretion.

bottomLine: The world is absorbing a gas shock and a coal revival at the same time. Germany's lignite spread has gone from zero to as much as $72 per MWh and South Korea's energy minister is openly telling his country to burn less LNG this winter, while Europe enters the season at 74% storage against an 86% five-year average and has quietly relaxed its own 90% mandate to 80%. Brent's slip to about $108 from Friday's five-month high is a pause, not a reversal — fuel oil premia near $50 a ton and vitiated Middle East and Russian refinery output say the product market is still the binding constraint. The buffers that exist are not European: China's storage at 80% plus a warm El Niño forecast may spare everyone a cold-weather scramble. Meanwhile a German court is now hearing sworn evidence that Nord Stream was destroyed on behalf of Ukrainian state authorities, arriving in the same fortnight Washington floated Russian gas as a peace-deal currency. The next decisive variable is weather, not policy — and the policy options left are expensive, dirty, or both.
sources: OilPrice.com (Michael Kern, Tsvetana Paraskova, Irina Slav, Charles Kennedy, Cyril Widdershoven, Felicity Bradstock, RFE/RL staff), Bloomberg (via OilPrice.com), Reuters (via OilPrice.com), Energy Aspects, IEA Coal Mid-Year Update 2026, Rystad Energy, ING (Warren Patterson note), LSEG, Kpler, Vitol (Kieran Gallagher), Ember and Global Energy Monitor, Gas Infrastructure Europe (via Anadolu Agency), Anadolu Agency (AA Energy), Upstream, EU Institute for Security Studies, The Guardian, German Federal Prosecutor's Office (Generalbundesanwalt), ARD/Sueddeutsche Zeitung/Die Zeit (indictment reporting), Indian market reporting on Brent settlement
